blocks.text:
With dynamic instances (containers started and stopped by an orchestrator) addresses change constantly, so the balancer or gateway asks a **service registry** for the current instances. In **client-side discovery** (Spring Cloud LoadBalancer with Eureka or Consul) the caller fetches the list and balances itself. In **server-side discovery** a balancer or the platform does it: a Kubernetes `Service` gives a stable virtual IP and DNS name, and `kube-proxy` or the CNI distributes connections to ready pods.

### Worked trace

The program `MiniLb.java` is a working layer 7 reverse proxy built with the JDK: a load balancer on port 9000 forwards requests round robin to three back ends on ports 9001 to 9003, adds `X-Forwarded-For`, and skips instances that a health check has marked down. The back end then stops, first without and then with the health check, to show the detection window.

blocks.title: MiniLb.java

blocks.code:
$ java MiniLb.java
-- round robin, all healthy
200 backend:9001 saw X-Forwarded-For=127.0.0.1 Host=127.0.0.1:9001
200 backend:9002 saw X-Forwarded-For=127.0.0.1 Host=127.0.0.1:9002
200 backend:9003 saw X-Forwarded-For=127.0.0.1 Host=127.0.0.1:9003
200 backend:9001 saw X-Forwarded-For=127.0.0.1 Host=127.0.0.1:9001
-- 9002 stopped, before the health check runs
502 bad gateway
200 backend:9003 saw X-Forwarded-For=127.0.0.1 Host=127.0.0.1:9003
200 backend:9001 saw X-Forwarded-For=127.0.0.1 Host=127.0.0.1:9001
502 bad gateway
-- after the health check marks 9002 down
200 backend:9003 saw X-Forwarded-For=127.0.0.1 Host=127.0.0.1:9003
200 backend:9001 saw X-Forwarded-For=127.0.0.1 Host=127.0.0.1:9001
200 backend:9003 saw X-Forwarded-For=127.0.0.1 Host=127.0.0.1:9003
200 backend:9001 saw X-Forwarded-For=127.0.0.1 Host=127.0.0.1:9001
blocks.title: Output of MiniLb.java

blocks.text:
What to notice, in order:

1. The requests rotate 9001, 9002, 9003 (round robin), and the balancer opens its own connection to each back end; the client never sees the back-end address.
2. `X-Forwarded-For=127.0.0.1` is the address of the original client, supplied by the proxy. Without this header the back end would see only the balancer address. The back end sees `Host=127.0.0.1:9001`, the back-end authority, because this proxy builds a new request; production proxies copy the original `Host` (nginx: `proxy_set_header Host` `$host;`) so that virtual hosting and redirect generation keep working.
3. After the 9002 instance stops and before any probe has run, every turn of the rotation that selects 9002 yields `502` `bad gateway` (connection refused): one request in three fails, here the first and the fourth of the four requests. A balancer reports a back-end connection failure with 502, and 504 when the back end accepted the connection but did not answer within the timeout.
4. After the health check marks 9002 down, requests alternate between 9003 and 9001 and no error is returned. Clients see a failure only during the detection window, which is why balancers combine active checks with passive ejection and **retry** idempotent requests on another instance.

### Hands-on

#### nginx as reverse proxy and load balancer

The configuration below (reference, not run here because nginx is not installed on the build machine) terminates TLS, balances two Spring Boot instances with least connections, passes the client address and original host, and sets timeouts and passive health checking.

blocks.title: nginx.conf (not run)

blocks.text:
Directives that matter: `least_conn` selects the algorithm (`ip_hash` and `hash $request_uri consistent;` give affinity and consistent hashing); `max_fails` and `fail_timeout` implement passive health checks; `keepalive` reuses back-end connections and avoids a TCP handshake per request; `proxy_next_upstream` retries only on connection errors, timeouts and the listed status codes. `proxy_next_upstream` does not retry non-idempotent methods by default, which prevents duplicate `POST` requests.

#### Spring Boot behind a proxy

Because the application sees the proxy address, redirects and generated links would use `http://` and the internal host unless the forwarded headers are honoured. In Spring Boot the setting `server.forward-headers-strategy=framework` (or `native` for the container implementation) makes `request.getRemoteAddr()`, `isSecure()` and generated URLs reflect `X-Forwarded-For`, `X-Forwarded-Proto` and `X-Forwarded-Host`. The headers must be trusted only when they come from the proxy: a client can send its own `X-Forwarded-For`, so the proxy must overwrite or append and the application must not use the header for security decisions unless the immediate peer is a known proxy.

#### Spring Cloud Gateway

Spring Cloud Gateway is a reactive layer 7 gateway. A route consists of a predicate (which requests match) and filters (what happens to them). The YAML below sends `/api/orders/**` to a load-balanced service name resolved through discovery, limits the rate and retries idempotent requests. It is shown for reference and was not run here. The property namespace is `spring.cloud.gateway.server.webflux.*` in the 5.x line; earlier releases use `spring.cloud.gateway.routes`.

blocks.code:
spring:
  cloud:
    gateway:
      server:
        webflux:
          routes:
            - id: orders
              uri: lb://orders-service
              predicates:
                - Path=/api/orders/**
              filters:
                - StripPrefix=1
                - name: Retry
                  args:
                    retries: 2
                    methods: GET
                    statuses: BAD_GATEWAY, SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE
                - name: RequestRateLimiter
                  args:
                    redis-rate-limiter.replenishRate: 10
                    redis-rate-limiter.burstCapacity: 20
blocks.title: application.yml (not run)

blocks.text:
The `RequestRateLimiter` filter is a token bucket stored in Redis with the parameters `replenishRate` (tokens per second) and `burstCapacity` (bucket size), the same algorithm as in the previous chapter; `lb://` asks the discovery client for instances of `orders-service`.

### Failure modes

- **Detection window.** Between failure and the health check verdict, clients receive errors. Tune interval and threshold (for example probe every 5 s, down after 2 failures) and retry idempotent requests.
- **Health check that lies.** A liveness probe that only checks that the process answers keeps an instance whose database connection is broken in rotation. Readiness checks should include critical dependencies but not cascade (a database outage should not mark every instance of every service down).
- **Thundering herd after recovery.** A recovered instance with an empty cache and cold JIT receives a full share of traffic immediately. Use slow start (weight ramp-up) or gradual re-admission.
- **Idle timeout mismatch.** If the balancer idle timeout (for example 60 s) is shorter than the back-end keep-alive timeout, or the opposite, requests fail intermittently with 502 when a connection is closed at the moment it is reused. The back-end keep-alive timeout must be longer than the balancer idle timeout (Tomcat: `server.tomcat.keep-alive-timeout` and `server.tomcat.connection-timeout`).
- **Lost client address.** Logs and rate limits keyed on the balancer address penalise everyone at once. Use `X-Forwarded-For` (validated) or the PROXY protocol for layer 4.
- **Uneven distribution.** Long-lived connections (HTTP/2, gRPC, WebSocket) pin all requests of a client to one back end at layer 4, so new instances stay idle. Balance at layer 7 per request, or recycle connections periodically.
- **Single point of failure.** The balancer itself must be redundant: an active-passive pair with a virtual IP (VRRP), several instances behind anycast or DNS, or a managed cloud service.
- **Oversized headers and body limits.** Proxies enforce limits (nginx `client_max_body_size`, header buffer sizes) and answer `413` or `400` before the request reaches the application.

### Questions to expect

#### 1. What is the difference between a layer 4 and a layer 7 load balancer?

Layer 4 forwards connections on the basis of IP addresses and ports and never reads the payload; it is fast and protocol-agnostic. Layer 7 terminates the connection, reads the HTTP request and routes by host, path or header, with features such as TLS termination, retries, caching and rewriting, at higher CPU cost.

#### 2. Compare round robin and least connections.

Round robin rotates through servers and is fair for uniform, short requests. Least connections routes to the server with the fewest active connections and copes with uneven request durations, because a server stuck on slow requests receives fewer new ones.

#### 3. Why is consistent hashing used instead of hash mod N?

With `hash mod N` a change in N remaps most keys, which empties caches and breaks affinity. In a consistent hash ring only the keys adjacent to the added or removed server move (about 1/N of the keys), and virtual nodes make the distribution even.

#### 4. How do health checks work, and what is the difference between liveness and readiness?

The balancer probes each instance at an interval and removes it after consecutive failures; passive checks eject instances based on live errors. Liveness tells the orchestrator that the process must be restarted; readiness tells the balancer that the instance must not receive traffic yet or any more.

#### 5. What are sticky sessions and why are they avoided?

The balancer keeps a user on one instance, usually through a cookie. This is needed only when session state sits in instance memory. It leads to uneven load and lost sessions on failure or deployment, so shared session storage or stateless tokens are preferred.

#### 6. Where should TLS terminate?

At the edge balancer in most designs, to centralise certificates and allow HTTP-level routing. Where internal traffic must be protected, the balancer re-encrypts to the back end, ideally with mutual TLS; passthrough keeps TLS end to end but limits the balancer to layer 4.

#### 7. What does an API gateway do beyond load balancing?

It is the single entry point for APIs and applies authentication, rate limiting, routing, request transformation, response aggregation, circuit breaking, logging and tracing, so that services stay free of these concerns.

#### 8. A user receives intermittent 502 errors after a deployment. What is checked?

Back-end instances that were stopped while still in rotation (health check interval and connection draining), a keep-alive timeout of the back end shorter than the idle timeout of the balancer, application crashes at start-up, and back-end listen backlog or thread pool exhaustion.

#### 9. What is the difference between 502, 503 and 504?

502 means that the proxy received an invalid response or could not connect to the upstream; 503 means that the service or the proxy is unavailable or overloaded (no healthy back end); 504 means that the upstream did not answer within the proxy timeout.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- A reverse proxy represents servers; a load balancer distributes requests; an API gateway adds API policy. One product often does all three.
- Layer 4 balancing decides on addresses and ports and keeps TLS opaque; layer 7 terminates connections, reads HTTP and can route, retry and cache.
- Round robin suits uniform requests, least connections adapts to uneven ones, and consistent hashing moves only about 1/N of the keys when the server set changes.
- Health checks bound but do not remove the failure window; combine active and passive checks with retries of idempotent requests.
- TLS may terminate, pass through or be re-encrypted; always forward the client address and the original host and trust those headers only from the proxy.
- Keep-alive and idle timeouts must be consistent across the chain, or intermittent 502 responses result.

Two physical limits shape the delivery of web content: the propagation delay between a user and a distant server, and the capacity and reliability of a single data centre. A **content delivery network** (CDN) addresses the first by placing caching servers close to users. **High availability** (HA) addresses the second by removing single points of failure and by making clients and services tolerate the failures that remain. The two topics meet in one design principle: every component can fail, so every call needs a timeout, a bounded retry policy and a fallback.

### Concept and mechanism

#### How a CDN serves a request

A CDN is a geographically distributed set of **points of presence** (PoP), each with caching reverse proxies (**edge** **servers**). The site owner points the public name at the CDN, usually with a `CNAME` record (`www.example.com` to a CDN host name) or by moving the DNS zone to the CDN. The user is directed to a nearby PoP by DNS-based steering (the answer depends on the resolver location) or by anycast. The edge server looks up the object in its cache using a **cache** **key** (normally scheme, host, path and selected query parameters and headers). On a hit it answers from memory or disk; on a miss it fetches the object from the **origin**, stores it according to the response headers, and returns it. Large CDNs insert an **origin shield**, a regional cache that merges the misses of many edges so that the origin sees one request per object per shield.

blocks.text:
A CDN reduces latency (fewer round trips over long distances, and TCP and TLS connections terminate near the user), reduces origin load and bandwidth, and absorbs traffic spikes and denial-of-service floods because the edge capacity exceeds that of a single origin. Most CDNs also terminate TLS, speak HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 to browsers, and offer a web application firewall.

#### Cache control headers

Caching behaviour is controlled by response headers (HTTP caching is defined in RFC 9111; the validators `ETag` and `Last-Modified` were covered in the earlier Part on HTTP caching).

rows: The response is fresh for N seconds in any cache, including the browser.
Freshness for shared caches (CDN, proxy) only; overrides `max-age` there. Allows a long CDN lifetime and a short browser lifetime.
`private` forbids shared caches (per-user content); `public` permits them even for requests with an `Authorization` header.
The cache may store the response but must revalidate before every reuse.
Do not store the response at all (sensitive data).
After expiry, serve the stale copy for up to N seconds while refreshing in the background (RFC 5861).
Serve a stale copy for N seconds when the origin returns an error or is unreachable (RFC 5861).
The content will not change during its freshness lifetime; browsers skip revalidation on reload (RFC 8246).
The cache key also includes the named request headers; `Vary: Cookie` makes the cache nearly useless.
blocks.caption: Cache-Control directives that matter at the edge.

blocks.text:
A frequent production pattern is versioned asset names (`app.4f3a9c.js`) served with `Cache-Control: public,` `max-age=31536000, immutable`, while the HTML document that references them is served with `no-cache` or a short `s-maxage`. A new deployment changes the file name, so no purge is needed. Objects that must change at a known time are removed with the purge (invalidation) API of the CDN.

#### Anycast

With **anycast** the same IP address is announced by BGP from many locations. Each router forwards packets towards the topologically nearest announcement, so users reach the closest PoP without any DNS logic, and a PoP that fails withdraws its route and traffic moves to the next nearest one. Anycast is the standard for public DNS resolvers and CDN edges, and it spreads the traffic of a DDoS attack over many sites. The limitation is that a routing change in the middle of a long TCP connection can move packets to a different PoP, which then has no state for that connection and answers with a reset; for this reason anycast suits short connections and QUIC, and CDNs add connection-aware forwarding between PoPs.

blocks.text:
#### Redundancy and failover

High availability is obtained by redundancy at every tier, with failure detection and a switch-over mechanism.

- **Active-active**: all nodes serve traffic (instances behind a balancer, multiple availability zones). Capacity must allow for the loss of a node (N+1 or N+2).
- **Active-passive**: a standby takes over on failure. A pair of balancers or routers shares a virtual IP address through VRRP or keepalived; when the master stops sending advertisements (default interval one second, three missed advertisements) the backup claims the address and announces it with gratuitous ARP.
- **Multi-zone and multi-region**: independent failure domains. Cross-region designs add data replication and the difficulty of consistency.
- **Split brain**: if the link between the two nodes fails but both stay alive, both may claim to be active. Quorum or a third arbiter prevents it.

Failover can happen at the DNS layer or at the balancer layer, and the two differ greatly in speed. DNS failover changes the answer of a name when a health check fails, but resolvers and clients cache the old answer until the **TTL** expires, and some clients and JVMs cache longer than the TTL (the Java property `networkaddress.cache.ttl` and the security setting of the same name). Balancer-level failover (virtual IP, health-checked pool) switches in seconds because the address does not change.

blocks.text:
#### Timeouts, retries and backoff

Every network call needs a **timeout**, because a call that never completes holds a thread, a connection and memory. A **retry** repairs transient failures (packet loss, a restarting instance, a momentary overload), but retries multiply load, so they must be limited and spaced. The standard schedule is **exponential backoff** (delay doubles after each attempt up to a cap) with **jitter** (the delay is randomised, so that clients that failed together do not retry together). With full jitter the delay for attempt n is a uniform random value between 0 and min(cap, base x 2^n).

Retries are safe only for **idempotent** operations (see the REST chapter of the HTTP Part): `GET`, `PUT` and `DELETE` are idempotent by definition; `POST` is not, so retrying it can create duplicates. A client-generated **idempotency key** sent in a header (for example `Idempotency-Key: 7c9e6679`) allows the server to recognise a repeat and return the original result, which makes retrying a `POST` safe.

#### The retry storm

When a dependency slows down, every caller times out and retries. If three tiers each retry three times, one user request becomes 3 x 3 x 3 = 27 requests at the bottom tier, which is already overloaded. The extra load keeps it down after the original cause has gone: the failure is sustained by the retries (a **metastable failure**). The countermeasures are layered.

- Retry at one layer only (usually the one closest to the user), never at every tier.
- Cap retries with a **retry budget** (for example retries may not exceed 10 percent of the request rate).
- Use exponential backoff with jitter.
- Use a **circuit breaker** to stop calls to a failing dependency.
- Propagate a deadline, so that work for a caller that has already given up is dropped.
- Shed load at the server (return 503 quickly) instead of queueing unboundedly.

blocks.text:
#### Circuit breakers

A **circuit breaker** wraps calls to a dependency and tracks their outcomes. In the **closed** state calls pass through. When failures exceed a threshold the breaker **opens**: calls fail at once (or return a fallback) without touching the dependency, which relieves it and avoids holding threads for the full timeout. After a wait period the breaker becomes **half-open** and allows a few trial calls; if they succeed it closes, otherwise it opens again.

blocks.text:
### Worked trace

#### An edge cache with real headers

The program implements a miniature CDN edge: an origin on port 9201 sends `Cache-Control: public, max-age=2` and a body that contains a version counter; an edge on port 9200 caches responses by path and honours `max-age`. A client requests the same path five times with pauses, and the edge adds `X-Cache` and `Age` headers.

blocks.title: EdgeCache.java

blocks.code:
$ java EdgeCache.java
request 1: X-Cache=MISS Age=0 body="price list v1" origin hits so far=1
request 2: X-Cache=HIT Age=1 body="price list v1" origin hits so far=1
request 3: X-Cache=HIT Age=1 body="price list v1" origin hits so far=1
request 4: X-Cache=MISS Age=0 body="price list v2" origin hits so far=2
request 5: X-Cache=HIT Age=0 body="price list v2" origin hits so far=2
blocks.title: Output of EdgeCache.java

blocks.text:
Reading the result: request 1 finds an empty cache (`MISS`) and fills it from the origin. Requests 2 and 3, at 1.1 s and 1.7 s, are served from the edge (`HIT`) with a growing `Age`, and the origin hit counter does not change. Request 4 arrives at 2.7 s, after the two-second lifetime, so the edge fetches again (`MISS`, version 2). Request 5 is a hit once more. A real edge would also store `ETag`, send `If-None-Match` and accept a `304` to refresh without transferring the body, as in the sequence diagram.

#### Backoff and jitter

The program computes the delays of exponential backoff (base 100 ms, doubling, cap 5,000 ms) with and without full jitter, and compares the timing of the third retry of 1,000 clients that all failed at time 0.

blocks.title: Backoff.java

blocks.code:
$ java Backoff.java
attempt  plain-delay-ms  full-jitter-sample-ms
      1             100                     73
      2             200                    149
      3             400                    139
      4             800                    717
      5            1600                   1133
      6            3200                   1126
no jitter  : third retry of 1000 clients lands in 1 distinct 50 ms windows, peak 1000
full jitter: third retry of 1000 clients lands in 13 distinct 50 ms windows, peak 141
Layered retries: 3 attempts at each of 3 tiers = 27 calls reach the database per user request
blocks.title: Output of Backoff.java

blocks.text:
Without jitter the whole population retries at the same instant (here 100 + 200 + 400 = 700 ms): the dependency sees a synchronised spike of 1,000 requests. With full jitter the same retries are spread over 13 windows with a maximum of

1. The jitter samples vary with the random seed; the figures above are for seed 7.

#### A circuit breaker under a dependency outage

The simulation drives a breaker (open after 3 consecutive failures, stay open for 2,000 ms) with one call every 500 ms. The dependency is down between 2,000 ms and 6,000 ms. The state column shows the state before each call.

blocks.title: Breaker.java

blocks.code:
$ java Breaker.java
t=   0 ms  dependency up    CLOSED    -> success
t= 500 ms  dependency up    CLOSED    -> success
t=1000 ms  dependency up    CLOSED    -> success
t=1500 ms  dependency up    CLOSED    -> success
t=2000 ms  dependency DOWN  CLOSED    -> failure 1 (timeout after 2000 ms)
t=2500 ms  dependency DOWN  CLOSED    -> failure 2 (timeout after 2000 ms)
t=3000 ms  dependency DOWN  CLOSED    -> failure 3, circuit OPEN
t=3500 ms  dependency DOWN  OPEN      -> rejected immediately (OPEN)
t=4000 ms  dependency DOWN  OPEN      -> rejected immediately (OPEN)
t=4500 ms  dependency DOWN  OPEN      -> rejected immediately (OPEN)
t=5000 ms  dependency DOWN  OPEN      -> probe failed, circuit OPEN again
t=5500 ms  dependency DOWN  OPEN      -> rejected immediately (OPEN)
t=6000 ms  dependency up    OPEN      -> rejected immediately (OPEN)
t=6500 ms  dependency up    OPEN      -> rejected immediately (OPEN)
t=7000 ms  dependency up    OPEN      -> probe succeeded, circuit CLOSED
t=7500 ms  dependency up    CLOSED    -> success
t=8000 ms  dependency up    CLOSED    -> success
t=8500 ms  dependency up    CLOSED    -> success
t=9000 ms  dependency up    CLOSED    -> success
blocks.title: Output of Breaker.java

blocks.text:
What to notice. The three failures between 2,000 and 3,000 ms each cost a full timeout. After the breaker opens, calls at 3,500, 4,000 and 4,500 ms are rejected immediately and cost nothing. At 5,000 ms the wait has elapsed and a trial call is sent, which fails because the dependency is still down, so the breaker reopens. At 7,000 ms the next trial call succeeds and the circuit closes. During the four seconds of outage the dependency receives four calls (three failures that opened the breaker and one trial call) instead of eight, and recovery is detected one wait period after the dependency returns.

#### Retries and circuit breakers with Resilience4j

In a Spring Boot service the retry and breaker policies are normally configured rather than hand-coded. The properties below (Resilience4j Spring Boot starter, reference sample, not run) define a breaker that opens when half of the last 20 calls fail, waits 10 seconds, and a retry policy of three attempts with exponential backoff and randomisation.

blocks.code:
resilience4j.circuitbreaker.instances.inventory.sliding-window-size=20
resilience4j.circuitbreaker.instances.inventory.failure-rate-threshold=50
resilience4j.circuitbreaker.instances.inventory.wait-duration-in-open-state=10s
resilience4j.circuitbreaker.instances.inventory.permitted-number-of-calls-in-half-open-state=3
resilience4j.retry.instances.inventory.max-attempts=3
resilience4j.retry.instances.inventory.wait-duration=200ms
resilience4j.retry.instances.inventory.enable-exponential-backoff=true
resilience4j.retry.instances.inventory.exponential-backoff-multiplier=2
resilience4j.retry.instances.inventory.enable-randomized-wait=true

blocks.text:
#### Failover checks

To measure real failover behaviour, stop one instance and watch the client: the time until errors cease is the detection interval plus, for DNS, the TTL. The JVM caches successful lookups for 30 seconds by default when no security manager is installed (`networkaddress.cache.ttl` in `java.security`, default 30 in recent JDKs), and failed lookups for 10 seconds (`networkaddress.cache.negative.ttl`); services that depend on DNS failover must set these values explicitly, for example to 10 seconds, with the system property `-Dsun.net.inetaddr.ttl=10` or in the `java.security` file.

### Failure modes

- **Cache poisoning of personalised content.** A response containing user data cached as `public` and served to other users. Symptom: users see each other pages. Prevention: `private` or `no-store` for personalised responses; `Vary` only on stable headers.
- **Cache fragmentation.** Tracking parameters, cookies or `Vary: Cookie` give every request a unique key and a zero hit ratio, so all traffic reaches the origin. Normalise the cache key.
- **Stale content after deployment.** Long lifetimes without versioned names or purge. Use content-hashed file names for assets and short or revalidated lifetimes for HTML.
- **Cache stampede.** When a popular object expires, many edges and requests hit the origin at once. Mitigation: request collapsing at the edge, origin shield, `stale-while-revalidate`, jittered lifetimes.
- **Failover slower than expected.** DNS TTLs and client-side caches delay switch-over far beyond the health-check interval. Lower the TTL before planned changes and verify resolver behaviour in the client runtime.
- **Retry storm.** Described above. Symptom: load stays high after the original fault has been fixed; remedy: remove retries at inner tiers, add budgets and jitter, shed load.
- **Timeouts longer than the caller deadline.** A service that waits 30 seconds for a dependency while its own caller gives up after 5 seconds keeps working for nobody. Inner timeouts must be shorter than outer ones.
- **Untested failover.** A standby that has never taken traffic often fails to do so (missing configuration, expired certificate, cold cache). Exercise failover regularly.
- **Breaker misconfiguration.** A threshold that is too sensitive opens on normal error noise; a wait period that is too long keeps a recovered dependency isolated.

### Questions to expect

#### 1. How does a CDN reduce latency?

It serves content from an edge server near the user, so the request travels a short distance and TCP and TLS handshakes complete over a short round-trip time; cache hits avoid the origin entirely, and the edge keeps warm connections to the origin for misses.

#### 2. Explain `max-age`, `s-maxage` and `no-cache`.

`max-age` sets freshness in seconds for all caches; `s-maxage` does so for shared caches only and overrides `max-age` there; `no-cache` allows storage but requires revalidation (for example with `If-None-Match`) before each reuse, whereas `no-store` forbids storage.

#### 3. What is anycast and what is its weakness?

One address is announced from many sites and routing delivers packets to the nearest. It gives low latency, automatic failover and distribution of attack traffic. A routing change during a long TCP connection can send later packets to a different site that has no state for the connection.

#### 4. DNS failover versus load balancer failover?

DNS failover changes the answer after a failed health check but is delayed by the TTL and by client caches (minutes). A load balancer or virtual IP keeps the address and removes the failed instance in seconds. Both are often combined: DNS or anycast selects the site, a balancer selects the instance.

#### 5. What is a retry storm and how is it prevented?

A slowdown causes timeouts, retries add load, and the extra load prolongs the slowdown. Layered retries multiply (3 x 3 x 3 = 27). Prevention: retry at one layer, use exponential backoff with jitter, limit retries with a budget, use circuit breakers and propagate deadlines.

#### 6. Why add jitter to backoff?

Clients that fail together would otherwise retry together at 100, 300 and 700 ms and produce synchronised spikes. Random delays spread the retries over time, which lowers the peak load on the recovering service.

#### 7. Which requests may be retried automatically?

Idempotent ones: `GET`, `HEAD`, `PUT`, `DELETE` and `OPTIONS`. A `POST` may be retried only if the server supports an idempotency key. A retry after a timeout is ambiguous, because the first attempt may have succeeded.

#### 8. Describe the states of a circuit breaker.

Closed: calls pass and failures are counted. Open: calls fail fast without reaching the dependency. Half-open after a wait: a few trial calls decide whether to close the breaker (success) or reopen it (failure).

#### 9. What is split brain and how is it avoided?

Two nodes of an active-passive pair both believe that they are active, usually after the link between them fails. Quorum (an odd number of voters), a witness node or fencing (power or network isolation of the other node) prevent it.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- A CDN serves cached content from nearby edges; behaviour is governed by `Cache-Control` (`max-age`, `s-maxage`, `stale-while-revalidate`) and `Vary`; versioned asset names avoid purges.
- Anycast routes users to the nearest PoP and removes failed sites by BGP withdrawal; DNS failover is bounded below by TTL and client caches.
- High availability needs redundancy, health checks and rehearsed failover; a virtual IP fails over in seconds, DNS in minutes.
- Every call needs a timeout; retries need backoff with jitter, budgets and idempotency; inner timeouts are shorter than outer ones.
- Layered retries multiply load (27 calls from 3 x 3 x 3) and sustain outages; circuit breakers and load shedding break the cycle.

In a monolith, a method call costs nanoseconds and fails only when the process fails. In a system of microservices the same call crosses a network: it costs milliseconds, can be slow, lost, duplicated or answered after the caller has given up, and it can fail while the caller and callee are both healthy. Network design for microservices consists of choosing how services find and call each other, bounding every wait, reusing connections economically, and making latency visible. The classic list of assumptions that do not hold (the network is reliable, latency is zero, bandwidth is infinite, the topology does not change) summarises the problem.

### Concept and mechanism

#### North-south and east-west traffic

**North-south** traffic crosses the boundary of the cluster: a browser or mobile client talks to a gateway or ingress. **East-west** traffic stays inside: service to service, service to database, cache or message broker. A single external request usually fans out to several internal calls, so east-west traffic volume commonly exceeds north-south traffic by a large factor. The two have different controls: north-south traffic needs TLS from the public Internet, authentication, rate limiting and a WAF at the gateway; east-west traffic needs service identity (mutual TLS), authorisation between services, short timeouts and retries, and network policies that restrict which service may call which.

blocks.text:
#### Service-to-service calls and discovery

Services call each other synchronously (HTTP/JSON, gRPC) or asynchronously through a broker (Kafka, RabbitMQ). Synchronous calls are simple but couple availability and latency: the caller is slow when the callee is slow. Asynchronous messaging decouples the two at the cost of eventual consistency and operational complexity.

In Kubernetes a `Service` gives a set of pods a stable name and virtual IP: `orders.shop.svc.cluster.local` resolves to a cluster IP, and `kube-proxy` (iptables or IPVS rules) or the CNI distributes each new **connection** to a ready pod. Two consequences matter for Java clients. First, distribution is per connection, not per request: an HTTP/1.1 client with a keep-alive pool or a gRPC client with one long-lived HTTP/2 connection keeps talking to the same pod, so a scaled-up deployment may receive no traffic from existing clients. Second, a **headless service** (`clusterIP: None`) returns the pod addresses in DNS, which allows client-side balancing, subject to the JVM DNS cache (see the previous chapter). Alternatives are a layer 7 proxy or a service mesh that balances per request.

#### Fan-out and tail latency

If a request calls n services in parallel and waits for all of them, the request is slow whenever any one call is slow. When each call exceeds its 99th-percentile latency in 1 percent of cases, the probability that at least one of n calls is in the slow tail is 1 - 0.99^n.

headers: Each call slow in 1 percent of cases
Each call slow in 0.1 percent of cases
blocks.caption: Probability that a fan-out request meets at least one slow call.

blocks.text:
The calculation (1 - 0.99^n, 1 - 0.999^n) assumes independent calls. It explains why p99 and p99.9 of individual services matter more than their averages once calls are chained or fanned out, and why timeouts and hedged requests are applied to the tail.

#### Timeouts and deadlines

A client call has several distinct waiting phases, each with its own timeout.

- **Connect timeout**: establishing the TCP connection (and often the TLS handshake). Fails when the peer or a firewall does not answer the SYN. A refused connection fails at once; a filtered one waits for the full timeout.
- **Pool acquisition timeout**: waiting for a free connection from the client pool.
- **Read (response) timeout**: waiting for response data after the request was sent. This detects a peer that accepted the connection and then stalled.
- **Total deadline**: the upper bound for the whole operation including retries.

Without explicit values many libraries wait indefinitely (the JDK `HttpClient` blocks forever when a request has no `timeout`, as stated in its documentation) or for very long periods (operating-system TCP defaults). Timeouts must **nest**: each inner call must be given less time than the caller will wait, otherwise the callee works for a caller that has already given up. Many frameworks therefore propagate a **deadline** (gRPC does it natively) so that each hop knows the remaining budget.

blocks.text:
#### Connection pools and keep-alive

Creating a connection costs a TCP handshake (one round trip), a TLS handshake (one more in TLS 1.3, two in TLS 1.2) and a slow-start phase. A **connection pool** keeps connections open and reuses them for later requests; HTTP/1.1 keep-alive and HTTP/2 multiplexing make this possible. A pool needs three decisions.

1. **Size.** By Little's law the number of requests in flight equals throughput times latency. A service that sends 500 requests per second to a dependency whose calls take 40 ms holds 500 x 0.040 = 20 connections busy on average. A pool of 20 is exactly at saturation, so the pool is sized with headroom for variation (for example 30 to 50), and the dependency must tolerate the sum of the pools of all callers.
2. **Idle eviction.** Connections idle for longer than the idle timeout of the server, load balancer or NAT device are closed by that device without notice. The client must close idle connections earlier than the shortest timeout on the path, or the next request fails with a connection reset.
3. **Maximum lifetime.** Recycling connections after some minutes lets a client discover new instances behind a Kubernetes Service or DNS name and rebalance load.

#### Service mesh and sidecars

A **service mesh** moves network concerns out of application code into a **sidecar proxy** (typically Envoy) that runs next to every service instance and intercepts its traffic. The application calls `localhost` or the service name; the sidecars establish mutual TLS between themselves with short-lived workload certificates issued by the mesh control plane, and implement retries, timeouts, circuit breaking, load balancing per request and uniform metrics and tracing. The benefit is uniform policy for services written in any language and encrypted, authenticated east-west traffic without changes to the code. The costs are extra proxy hops (typically a few milliseconds per call), memory and CPU per pod, and the operational complexity of the control plane; sidecarless designs and Spring Cloud / Resilience4j libraries are alternatives.

blocks.text:
#### Observing network latency

Latency problems are found with measurements, not with guesses. Three kinds of data are needed.

- **Metrics**: for each route and dependency the rate of requests, the error rate and the duration as a **histogram** (the RED method). Percentiles (p50, p95, p99) are derived from histograms; averages hide the tail. Spring Boot with Micrometer records `http.server.requests` and `http.client.requests` and, with the appropriate settings, connection pool statistics.
- **Distributed traces**: a trace identifier created at the gateway is propagated on every call, so one request can be followed across services and the time spent in each hop and in each network wait is visible. The W3C **Trace** **Context** standard defines the `traceparent` header, for example `traceparent:` `00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01` (version, 16-byte trace id, 8-byte parent span id, flags).
- **Logs** that carry the trace id, so that log lines of one request can be joined.

At the network level, TCP statistics such as retransmissions and round-trip time per connection (`ss -ti` on Linux, not available on the build machine) show whether a slow call was caused by the network or by the application.

### Worked trace

#### Why the average hides the problem

The program starts a local server whose handler answers in 5 ms in 97 percent of cases and in 120 ms in 3 percent of cases (a stand-in for garbage-collection pauses, cold caches or slow disks), then sends 400 sequential requests with `HttpClient` and reports the distribution.

blocks.title: Latency.java

blocks.code:
$ java Latency.java
calls=400 mean=11.3 ms p50=6.9 ms p95=11.1 ms p99=126.5 ms max=203.4 ms
blocks.title: Typical output of Latency.java (measured on the build machine; varies between runs)

blocks.text:
The mean is close to the typical latency and hides the problem: roughly one call in thirty takes about twenty times longer than the median. The 99th percentile exposes it. For a request that fans out to many such services the table of the previous section applies: with 3 percent slow calls per service, a request calling 20 of them in parallel meets at least one slow call with probability 1 - 0.97^20, about 46 percent.

#### Connection reuse and per-request timeouts

The next program shows two facts with real numbers. The server reports the client port of each request. A single `HttpClient` reuses one TCP connection for sequential requests (same client port). A new client for every request opens a new connection each time (a new port each time), which is what happens when a client object is created per call. The last step shows a per-request timeout: the handler sleeps 1,500 ms and the request allows 500 ms.

blocks.title: Pool.java

blocks.code:
$ java Pool.java
One HttpClient, sequential requests (keep-alive):
  request 1 -> client port 51230
  request 2 -> client port 51230
  request 3 -> client port 51230
A new HttpClient (and so a new connection) per request:
  request 1 -> client port 51238
  request 2 -> client port 51242
  request 3 -> client port 51248
per-request timeout after about 500 ms: HttpTimeoutException: request timed out
blocks.title: Output of Pool.java (client ports vary between runs)

blocks.text:
What to notice. In the first loop all three requests arrive from the same client port: one TCP connection, one handshake. In the second loop each request comes from a new ephemeral port, so each paid a handshake (and, on a real network, a TLS handshake), and each left a connection in `TIME_WAIT` on the side that closed it. At high request rates a client that creates connections per request exhausts its ephemeral port range (about 28,000 ports on Linux by default); the symptom is `Cannot assign requested address`. The `HttpClient` object is therefore created once and shared. The final line shows `HttpTimeoutException`, the failure that a service must be prepared to handle on every call.

#### Pool sizing by Little's law

A worked example. A service handles 500 requests per second at peak and each request calls a dependency that answers in 40 ms at the median and 200 ms at p99.

1. Average connections busy: 500 x 0.040 = 20.
2. During a slowdown to 200 ms the same rate needs 500 x 0.200 = 100 connections.
3. A pool limited to 30 connections then queues requests; the waiting time adds to every call until the pending-acquire timeout fires.
4. With 10 instances of the service the dependency must accept up to 10 x 100 = 1,000 connections in the slow case.

Consequences: the pool limit protects the dependency (a bulkhead) but turns a slowdown into queueing at the caller, so the acquisition timeout must be short and the failure handled; and the capacity of the dependency (its own connection limit, for example a database `max_connections`) is part of the same calculation.

### Hands-on

#### Timeouts and pools in Spring Boot

Spring Boot 3.2 and later provide `RestClient`; the reference documentation for the current Spring Boot 4.x line configures timeouts globally with `spring.http.clients.connect-timeout` and `spring.http.clients.read-timeout` (earlier 3.x releases use a different prefix, so the reference of the Spring Boot version in use should be consulted). The sample below (not run here) sets them explicitly in code and shows a `WebClient` with a bounded Reactor Netty pool.

blocks.title: HttpClientConfig.java (not run)

blocks.text:
The Reactor Netty reference states that the default pool size of a `ConnectionProvider` built without settings is 2 x the number of processors (minimum 16) and that the default pending acquire timeout is 45 seconds, which is far longer than any user request should wait; both defaults deserve explicit values.

#### Keep-alive tuning

Keep-alive timeouts must decrease along the path from the client to the server for idle connections to be closed by the client first.

rows: Shorter than every device on the path
Load balancer or NAT idle timeout
60 s to 350 s depending on product
Longer than the caller idle time
Longer than the balancer idle timeout if the balancer reuses connections to the server
blocks.caption: Typical idle timeouts that must be ordered consistently (illustrative values).

blocks.text:
If the order is reversed, the server or a middlebox silently closes a connection at the moment the client sends a request on it, and the request fails with a reset or `502`. The error is intermittent and appears at low traffic, when connections stay idle.

#### Network policies

East-west access can be restricted in Kubernetes with `NetworkPolicy` objects, which a supporting CNI enforces. The policy below (reference, not run) allows only pods labelled `app: orders` to reach the inventory pods on port 8080.

blocks.code:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: inventory-allow-orders
  namespace: shop
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: inventory
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
    - from:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: orders
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 8080
blocks.title: networkpolicy.yaml (not run)

blocks.text:
### Failure modes

- **No timeouts.** A single slow dependency holds threads or connections of every caller until the pool is exhausted, and the failure spreads upwards (cascading failure). Every outbound call needs connect, read and acquisition timeouts.
- **Pool exhaustion.** Symptoms: latency grows while CPU stays low, then `pending acquire` or `Timeout waiting for` `connection from pool` exceptions. Diagnosis: pool metrics (active, idle, pending). Fix: size from Little's law, shorten timeouts, add a circuit breaker.
- **Connection per request.** A client object or connection created for every call exhausts ephemeral ports and CPU (TLS handshakes) and leaves many `TIME_WAIT` sockets. Reuse one client.
- **Stale DNS or stale connections.** After a deployment or scale event, clients keep connecting to removed pod addresses through cached DNS answers or long-lived connections. Use a bounded `networkaddress.cache.ttl`, maximum connection lifetime and readiness-based endpoints.
- **Idle connection reset.** Intermittent resets on the first request after a quiet period; cause: idle timeout ordering (see the table above).
- **Unbalanced load with long-lived connections.** gRPC and HTTP/2 clients pin to one pod behind a layer 4 Service. Use a headless Service with client-side balancing, a layer 7 proxy or a mesh.
- **Chatty services.** A request that makes dozens of sequential internal calls (the N+1 pattern across services) multiplies latency. Batch calls, aggregate in a gateway or backend-for-frontend, cache, or change the service boundaries.
- **Retry amplification and thundering herd.** Covered in the previous chapter: limit retries, add jitter and budgets.
- **Large payloads and head-of-line blocking.** Big responses over a shared HTTP/1.1 connection delay small ones; large JSON bodies cost serialisation time. Use pagination, compression, HTTP/2 or binary protocols where appropriate.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: Teams often discover their timeout policy during an incident. A typical post-incident finding: the gateway timeout was 30 seconds, the service-to-service timeout 60 seconds and the database timeout unlimited, so slow queries kept thousands of threads busy for work whose callers had left long before. The remedy is a written timeout budget per tier, enforced by configuration review and by chaos tests that inject latency.

### Questions to expect

#### 1. What is the difference between north-south and east-west traffic?

North-south traffic enters or leaves the cluster (client to gateway). East-west traffic flows between services inside it. East-west traffic is usually larger because of fan-out, and is secured with mutual TLS, network policies and service-level authorisation rather than perimeter controls alone.

#### 2. Which timeouts should every HTTP client configure?

A connect timeout, a read (response) timeout, and a pool acquisition timeout, plus an overall deadline that includes retries. Defaults are often infinite or very long. Inner timeouts must be shorter than the timeout of the caller.

#### 3. Why do p99 latencies matter more in microservices?

A request that depends on many calls meets a slow tail call with probability 1 - (1 - q)^n. With a 1 percent tail and 20 parallel calls, that is about 18 percent of requests, so tail behaviour of dependencies dominates user-visible latency.

#### 4. How is a connection pool sized?

From Little's law: connections in use = request rate x latency. Add headroom for latency variation, limit the total across all callers to what the dependency can accept, and set a short acquisition timeout so that exhaustion fails fast.

1. **5. A Kubernetes Service has three pods but one receives all the traffic from a gRPC client. Why?**

The Service balances per TCP connection. A gRPC client keeps one HTTP/2 connection open and multiplexes all calls over it, so all calls reach the pod that accepted that connection. Solutions: a headless Service with client-side balancing, a layer 7 proxy or mesh that balances per request, or periodic connection recycling.

#### 6. What does a service mesh provide and what does it cost?

It provides mutual TLS, retries, timeouts, circuit breaking, per-request balancing and uniform telemetry through sidecar proxies, without code changes. The costs are added latency per hop, resource overhead per pod and the complexity of operating the control plane.

#### 7. Why do intermittent connection resets appear on idle services?

An intermediary or the server closed an idle connection (idle timeout) and the client reused it. The client pool idle time must be shorter than the idle timeouts along the path, or connections must be validated before reuse.

#### 8. How is network latency observed in a Spring Boot system?

Micrometer histograms for server and client requests (percentiles per route and dependency), distributed tracing with W3C `traceparent` propagation, logs correlated by trace id, and pool and TCP metrics (retransmissions, RTT). Averages alone are not used because they hide the tail.

#### 9. Synchronous call or message broker?

Synchronous calls suit queries that need an immediate answer, at the price of coupled availability and latency. A broker decouples producer and consumer in time and absorbs bursts, suits notifications and workflows, and introduces eventual consistency, duplicates (consumers must be idempotent) and a new component to operate.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Every microservice call is a network call: it can be slow, fail while both sides are healthy, or complete after the caller has given up; design for partial failure.
- Configure connect, read and acquisition timeouts on every client, and make timeouts nest so that inner calls fail before outer ones.
- Reuse connections through a shared client and size pools with Little's law; order idle timeouts so that the client closes idle connections first.
- Fan-out makes tail latency dominate: with 20 parallel calls and a 1 percent tail, 18 percent of requests are slow.
- Kubernetes Services balance per connection; long-lived HTTP/2 or gRPC connections need client-side or layer 7 balancing.
- Service meshes provide mTLS, retries and telemetry without code changes at the cost of extra hops and operational complexity.
- Measure latency with histograms, traces and correlated logs, and read percentiles rather than averages.
